extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary critics, and young English writers seeking practical guidance in poetic composition and criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance for composing poetry and for the practice of literary criticism: how to choose subjects, construct poems, subordinate expression, and use classical models rather than following ephemeral fashions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of subject / choose an excellent action
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet has in the first place to select an excellent action; actions which most powerfully appeal to the great primary human affections are the most fit for poetical representation. The date (modern or ancient) of an action is irrelevant to its fitness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer actions that unite greatness and passion and that move permanent human feelings. Examples cited: Achilles, Prometheus, Clytemnestra, Dido—these ancient personages remain more interesting than many modern subjects. Anti-pattern: choosing a trivial or merely contemporary incident because it is 'of present import.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate, particular representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Any accurate representation which is consistently drawn may be supposed to be interesting; what is not interesting is that which does not add to our knowledge—vague, indeterminate, and faint representations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make depictions particular, precise, and firm rather than general or loose. Accuracy of representation is a necessary foundation: avoid blurred or vague portrayals that fail to increase the reader's knowledge of the action or situation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetical enjoyment — art should inspirit and rejoice
rubrics_metrics.description: A poetical work must not only interest but also inspirit and rejoice the reader; the right art is that which creates the highest enjoyment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when representing tragic circumstances, aim to produce an aesthetic enjoyment; stronger tragedy can deepen enjoyment if handled as art. Anti-pattern: works that only inform without producing delight or emotional uplift.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid prolonged mental distress without action
rubrics_metrics.description: Situations in which suffering finds no vent in action, where continuous mental distress is prolonged without incident, hope, or resistance, are poetically faulty — they are monotonous and morbid rather than tragic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not base poems on stationary states of suffering with no outlet or resolution. Such subjects produce pain rather than dignified tragic enjoyment; prefer situations that allow action, resistance, or change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize action and total-impression over isolated expression
rubrics_metrics.description: The poetical whole (the action and its total-impression) should predominate over the brilliance of separate thoughts and images; modern tendency to value detached expressions over total effect is misguided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to produce a unified, total impression from the poem rather than a collection of striking lines. Anti-pattern: composing primarily to produce quotable sentences or occasional fine passages while neglecting overall composition and unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subordinate expression to matter; favor simplicity and clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Expression should be kept in its right degree of prominence; the ancients' expression is simple, well subordinated, and draws force from matter. Excessive or over-curious expression can impede the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer plain, direct language when the action demands it. Avoid over-elaboration, tortured or unnecessarily difficult phrasing (example: certain Shakespearean passages), which can obscure meaning and diminish the dramatic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful construction and adaptability of subject to poetic kind
rubrics_metrics.description: For all kinds of poetry, adaptability of the subject to the chosen kind of poetry and careful construction of the poem are essential; action should be constructed in the mind before lines are written.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan the action and its construction (Menander's practice of finishing the action before writing a line). Ensure the subject fits the poetic form (tragic subject for tragedy, comic for comedy) and that parts are subordinated to the whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek subjects that move permanent human passions
rubrics_metrics.description: The eternal objects of poetry are human actions that appeal to primary, permanent affections; the modernness of a subject does not determine its poetic fitness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose subjects whose essentials (inward feelings, passions in crisis) are accessible and powerful across time. Anti-pattern: privileging topicality or novelty over moral/grand emotional scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject the aim of allegory of one's own mind as highest poetic purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: The view that a poem should be 'a true allegory of the state of one's own mind' is false; such inward allegory is not the highest thing poetry can attempt and has not produced great poetical works as its dominant aim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not make self-allegory or introspective representation the principal goal of poetic art; ensure the work remains an imitation of human action rather than merely a record of personal mental states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn technical discipline from classical models
rubrics_metrics.description: The ancients teach three vitally important things to the modern writer: the all-importance of the choice of subject; the necessity of accurate construction; and the subordinate character of expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study classical works for clarity of arrangement, rigor of development, and simplicity of style. Use them as models for craft even if their externals differ from modern life—adopt their discipline rather than their narrow subject-matter where inappropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be wary of excessive imitation of a single model (Shakespeare) focused on expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Shakespeare's unrivalled gift of expression has led imitators to emphasize brilliant language and isolated passages at the expense of composition and action; this produces works valuable in detail but compositionally weak.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Shakespeare for inspiration but avoid copying his expressive exuberance to the detriment of unity and construction. Example/anti-pattern: Keats's 'Isabella' praised for felicitous expressions yet criticized here for loose construction where the same action is far more pregnant in the Decameron.

rubrics_metrics.name: The critic's role: temper violence and one-sidedness in public discourse
rubrics_metrics.description: Political or partisan discussion tends to become violent and one-sided; the work of criticism is to temper such fierceness and abstract system-building (Arnold: 'Culture is the eternal opponent of... Jacobinism—its fierceness and its addiction to an abstract system').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should cultivate coolness, freedom from bitterness, and balanced judgment; criticism ought to mitigate extremes in public argument and interpret perplexing periods for readers and writers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give due weight to critical work — criticism as necessary intellectual effort
rubrics_metrics.description: A principal intellectual effort of modern Europe has been the critical effort to 'see the object as in itself it really is'; criticism is an important cultural activity and not merely a lesser pursuit than creation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value critical practice as a distinct and necessary exercise that clarifies objects of thought and literature. Counter the view (e.g., Wordsworth's) that criticism is 'inglorious' and inferior to invention; good criticism steadies judgment and aids creative work.
